title: SQL Aggregation: GROUP BY, COUNT, SUM, AVG
oneLiner: Answering "how many" and "what's the average, per group" without writing a loop -- GROUP BY collapses many rows into one summary row per group.
keyTakeaway: Every column in the SELECT list has to be either something you GROUP BY or the result of an aggregate function (COUNT, SUM, AVG, MIN, MAX) -- mixing in a plain column that's neither is a common mistake, because the database has no way to know WHICH of the many rows in that group's plain column value you actually meant.
explanation:
COUNT(*), SUM(column), AVG(column), MIN(column), and MAX(column) are aggregate functions -- each one collapses many rows down to a single number. Used alone (`SELECT COUNT(*) FROM employees`), that number is computed across the WHOLE table. Add GROUP BY and it changes shape entirely: `GROUP BY department_id` splits all the rows into one bucket per distinct department_id first, THEN runs the aggregate separately within each bucket -- so COUNT(*) becomes "how many employees in EACH department," not one number for the whole company.

HAVING is WHERE's counterpart for GROUPS instead of individual rows -- filtering `WHERE salary > 100000` happens before grouping (on raw employee rows), while `HAVING COUNT(*) > 5` happens after grouping (on the summarized group rows). "Only show departments with more than 5 people" can only be expressed with HAVING, since "how many people" doesn't exist as a value until after the grouping already happened.
